title: Ladder Inspection & Setup

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Outside a one-story building with a soft grass strip at the wall. Extension ladder on the ground, a stepladder beside it. Danny medium shot.
scenes.says: Job Mindset for setting a ladder. The hazards: a ladder that fails, slides or kicks out, overhead lines, and doors or traffic hitting your ladder. Look up first, inspect it, set it right, and secure it. Plan before you leave: the right ladder, rope to tie off, cones, and a second person for anything over 30 feet. Think about where the ladder goes next.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.says: You inspect every ladder, every time you use it. Two minutes. A competent person also inspects our whole fleet every quarter, but you can retire a ladder any time you think it isn't safe. A ladder with a structural defect gets red-tagged DO NOT USE and comes out of service. Never repair a ladder in the field.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Senior tech goes down the stepladder with the company checklist, touching each item: feet, rungs, joints, rivets, hinges, spreaders, rails, labels. Danny voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Feet - Clean - Joints tight - Hardware - Moving parts - Spreaders - Rails - Edges - Labels - Non-skid steps
scenes.says: Here's our checklist. Non-slip feet on all four rails. No oil or grease. Joints tight. No loose rivets, bolts or nuts. Moving parts work without binding. Spreaders straight and locking. Rails and steps free of cracks, crushing, bends or splits. Metal ladders have their insulator pads. No sharp edges. Labels in place and legible. Non-skid surfaces on every step.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Tech checks the extension ladder rung locks, rope and pulley, spur spikes; then finds a cracked rail on a second ladder and hangs a red DO NOT USE tag. Danny voice-over.
scenes.says: On an extension ladder, add the rung locks, the rope and pulley, the guide brackets, and the swivel feet and spikes. On fiberglass, look for blooming, that's exposed glass fibers, and burn marks. This one's got a cracked rail. Red tag, out of service, tell the supervisor. And a ladder that's been dropped or fell off the rack gets inspected again before anyone climbs it.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Tech looks up at the roofline for overhead lines, then measures with a tape: 12 ft up the wall to the contact point, 3 ft out at the base. Graphic overlay of the 4:1 triangle.
scenes.on_screen: 4:1 rule: 12 ft up = 3 ft out. 10 ft from overhead lines.
scenes.says: Setting the extension ladder. Look up first for power lines. Stay at least 10 feet from lines up to 50 kV, and assume every line is live. Raise it with the fly retracted. Then the 4 to 1 rule: base out one-fourth of the height to the contact point. Our example is 12 feet up, 3 feet out. That's about 75 degrees.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Close-ups: spur spikes pushed into soft ground, both rung locks engaged, ladder top extending above the roof edge, rope tie-off at the top. Danny voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Access: 3 ft above the landing. Tie off against wind.
scenes.says: Soft ground? Use the spur spikes. Extend the fly with the rope and confirm both rung locks are engaged and the overlap on the label is met. If you're using it to get onto the roof, the rails go at least 3 feet above the landing. Then secure it. Tie off extension ladders so wind can't blow them down. Never lean it against a window or a pole without a pole strap.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Indoor hallway. Stepladder set up fully open next to a door that has been locked, with a sign posted and cones around the base.
scenes.on_screen: Never near a door that can open into it
scenes.says: Stepladder. Firm, level, dry, clear floor. Open it fully and push the spreaders down till they lock. All four feet flat, no rocking. Set it close to the work so your body stays between the rails. Never near a door that could open into it. Lock or block the door, and post a person or a sign. In aisles, cone it off. And never use a stepladder closed and leaned against a wall.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Danny strapping a ladder back onto the van rack.
scenes.on_screen: Put ladders away when not in use
scenes.says: When you're done with it, put it away. A ladder left standing is a trip hazard, an invitation for a customer to climb, and a target for carts and forklifts. Strap it back on the rack, and report any damage to the rack.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.on_screen: Now read the lesson and take the quiz
scenes.says: Inspect it, look up, set it at 4 to 1, secure it, and put it away. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Senior tech performs the inspection and setup on camera; Danny narrates. Film at a building with no overhead lines within 10 ft of the ladder. Props: company ladder inspection form, a ladder with a cracked rail already retired, red DO NOT USE tags, tape measure, tie-off rope, cones, door sign. Tie-off is shown at the top; tech must be properly positioned per the next lesson when climbing to tie.
